w:r.w:t: Barangay Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Plan

A barangay where every resident is empowered, prepared, and actively involved in building a safe, resilient, and thriving community, capable of mitigating risks and thriving in the face of any disaster.
To foster a culture of preparedness and resilience within the barangay, through collaborative efforts that prioritize:
Proactively identifying and mitigating disaster risks through community-based planning, infrastructure improvements, and education initiatives.
Equipping residents with the knowledge, skills, and resources to understand and manage risks, participate in preparedness activities, and support each other during emergencies.
Establishing robust systems and protocols for timely and efficient response to disasters, ensuring the safety and well-being of all residents.
Promoting rapid and equitable recovery from disasters, leveraging community resources and partnerships to rebuild stronger and more resilient infrastructure and livelihoods.
Engaging residents in all stages of disaster risk reduction, from planning and implementation to response and recovery.
Working closely with local government agencies, community organizations, private sector partners, and other stakeholders to leverage resources and expertise.
Utilizing data and technology to inform risk assessments, improve early warning systems, and optimize resource allocation.
Regularly evaluating disaster preparedness and response efforts, adapting to changing conditions, and seeking opportunities for improvement.

Long before Barangay Hinaplanon came into existence, the barrio was originally known as Tambo, a name derived from a tall grass called “tambo” which abundantly grew in the barangay. Barrio Tambo was then comprised of Hinaplanon,
. The areas were devoted to corn and sugar production.

In the early seventies, these areas were teemed with people. Sometimes in 1965, a law was sponsored by Vice-President Emmanuel Pelaez who was then a senator. The enactment of the law calls for the registration of all barrios in the Philippines as a prelude to the coming election of Barrio Officials particularly the Teniente del Barrio. Before the law, the Teniente del Barrio was appointed by the
. The incumbent Teniente del Barrio at that time was Mr.

Llanes, a resident of Hinaplanon. He had the name of the barrio registered as Hinaplanon, which surprises the residents of Tambo, through a Resolution Number 329, series of 1966 which was then enacted by the City Council of Iligan on January 20, 1967 and subsequently approved by the
mayor. Barangay Hinaplanon formally came into existence.
The name Hinaplanon was derived from the word “
”, a medicinal plant effective for the treatment of skin diseases of the children and other skin illnesses.

The principal products of the barangay were corn and sugar. There were four corn mills in Tambo and three in Hinaplanon. In the entire barangay, there were six local sugar mills. Other products were coconut and bananas. Fish were also abundant along the shore particularly in

The first barangay election for one year term of office of the Teniente del Barrio and five (5) councilmen was held in 1966 and the second was in 1967. In the 1968 election, the term of office of the Barrio Officials was increased to four (4) years. However, barrio officials who elected in 1968 were caught by the Declaration of Martial law in 1972 and they were on a holdover capacity until 1976, when an election was called for, to refresh the people’s mandate.
Influx of people in Iligan City were experienced. Attracted and lured by the booming industrialization of the

, people all over the country came over to work and settle down in the place. This tremendously affected the barangays of Iligan and particularly Hinaplanon. The fields devoted to corn and sugar were converted to highways, subdivisions and residential areas. Because of the increase in population in some places of the barangay, some residents agreed to create their own barangay and separate from the mother barangay which is Hinaplanon. This leads to the creation of Barangay

Despite the creation and separation of the four barangays, Barangay Hinaplanon still possesses a land area of 551.54 hectares with a population of 15,424 as of the year 2022. It has 23 puroks, has two Day care centers and a complete Elementary and Secondary schools, to answer the educational needs of the people.

The Barangay Disaster Risk Reduction Management Committee (BDRRMC) is one of the committees of the Barangay Development Council which is designated by law (RA 10121, otherwise known as the “Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010”) to oversee and facilitate the activities for the safety and security of the population living in the community. The committee is responsible for implementing programs, projects and activities within the community or barangay to prevent or minimize the impact of natural or human-induced hazards to people, property, business, critical facilities and infrastructure, environment and other elements at risk in the community.
The BDRRMC, under the Barangay Development Council, has the functions to be implemented in accordance with RA 10121. These are as follows:
To approve, monitor and assess the implementation of the barangay disaster risk reduction management plan in accordance to the city or municipal and other

Ensure that the disaster risk reduction and climate change adaptation will be integrated into the local development plans, activities, projects and programs and will be funded as strategy for sustainable development and poverty reduction in the community.
Recommend for the strict implementation of mandatory and forced evacuation if there is a threat to the people, especially those who are living in a high-risk zones or areas; and
Convene the committee and conduct quarterly meeting or as needed.

The committee consists of members of the council, representatives from education sector, church-based organization, civil-society organization and other vulnerable groups in the barangay. It is headed by the Punong Barangay as Chairperson. The following sectors should have an active and meaningful role in BDRRMC which is duly approved through an ordinance or resolution passed by the council.
sector or group in the barangay

The primary basis of the sectoral membership to BDRRMC is the legitimacy of the organizations with barangay programs or projects. A legitimate organization is duly registered, accredited to any authorized government agency or recognized by the Sangguniang Bayan or Barangay.

They must also actively participate in any barangay or community development activities. If they are not yet registered in any government agency, they may also submit a letter to the Sangguniang Barangay in order to identify them as a legitimate organization in the barangay.

A Community Risk Assessment (CRA) or sometimes called as Hazard, Vulnerability and Capacity Assessment (HVCA) is a process that uses a participatory approach which enables the community to Identify potential hazards and determine the nature and extent of risks they pose. It determines also the strengths and opportunities available within the barangay that will help us minimize or at least cope with these risks.

It is a means to collectively analyze community vulnerabilities, highlight capacities and identify gaps for integrated and strategic investment of resources to reduce their occurrence or impact to population, property and environment.
Processes and Contents of Community Risk Assessment (CRA)
Barangay Hinaplanon is one of the most densely populated barangays in Iligan City and lies along the flood-prone areas of the

River. The barangay covers 23 puroks, several of which are located in low-lying and riverbank areas, making them highly vulnerable to hydrometeorological hazards such as flooding, flash floods, and landslides.
On December 17, 2011, Barangay Hinaplanon was severely devastated by Typhoon
(Washi), which brought unprecedented rainfall that caused the

River to overflow, resulting in massive flash floods. This disaster claimed hundreds of lives, displaced thousands of families, and caused irreparable damage to infrastructure, homes, and livelihoods.

Given its geographical location, Hinaplanon remains at high risk for recurring flooding, particularly during the rainy season and in the event of tropical cyclones. Climate change has increased the unpredictability of these hazards, intensifying the urgency for proactive disaster risk reduction measures.
Other hazards identified in the barangay include:
proximity to the Western Mindanao Fault.
Fire incidents, especially in congested residential areas.
Health emergencies, such as outbreaks of waterborne diseases post-flooding.
s socio-economic vulnerability, including the presence of informal settlers in hazard zones and limited access to resilient infrastructure, further compounds its risk.

This risk profile underlines the need for continuous investment in disaster preparedness, infrastructure resilience, early warning systems, environmental protection, and capacity building among residents to reduce the long-term impact of future disasters.
